newsitem.title: USA: Intel warning sends stock sharply lower.
newsitem.headline: Intel warning sends stock sharply lower.

text.p: Intel Corp. , the leading maker of computer chips and a technology bellwether, stunned Wall Street on Friday by warning that its revenues and net income for the second quarter will fall below expectations due to weaker-than-projected demand.

The world's largest chipmaker, which in the past has managed to exceed Wall Street's expectations, said revenue for the period is expected to drop 5 to 10 percent below the first quarter's $6.4 billion, while gross margin, a key measure of profitability, is forecast at under the 64 percent of the prior period.
The news took Wall Street by surprise.

Intel's stock tumbled more than 12 percent in early trading on Nasdaq, with more than 12 million shares changing hands in the first hour of trading. It recovered slightly to trade at $149, off $14.766, or about 9 percent.

The selloff quickly spread to other stocks in the high-tech sector, with International Business Machines Corp. down $3.125 at $84.75 on the New York Stock Exchange and Micrsoft Corp. down as much as $8.375 at $117.50 a share on Nasdaq.
The Dow Jones industrial average felt the pressure as well, falling 84 points to 7,246. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index was down 44.6 points at 1,357.
At least one brokerage house weighed in with an immediate downgrade of Intel. Morgan Stanley cut its rating to outperform from strong buy.

"This is a bellwether event," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker. "Intel is such a force that to the extent that you use benchmarks, it is one of the benchmarks that you use."
"We're back where we were 10 days ago -- 10 too-good days ago," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd.
Intel provided few details for the shortfall, other than to say demand had weakened, particularly in Europe.
While the company said new products, such as the Pentium II processor, were experiencing strong demand, gross margins were expected to be 60 percent "plus or minus a few points."
That would mark a decline from the robust level of the first quarter, when gross margins hit 64 percent.
Over the long-term, the company said, it expected its gross margin percentage "will be 50 percent plus or minus a few points," in line with previous company forecasts.
In the second quarter of 1996, Intel reported a profit of $1.04 billion, or $1.17 a share, on revenues of $4.62 billion.
Prior to the company's outlook statement, analysts had expected Intel to report a second-quarter profit of $2.16 per share, according to a consensus of 35 analysts compiled by First Call.
Intel has benefited in the past from the strong acceptance of its Pentium processors, particularly from businesses looking to upgrade to more powerful computers.

The Santa Clara, Calif.-based company has had a virtual lock on the market, with more than 80 percent of the world's computers using Intel chips. As such, Intel is widely regarded as a lightning rod for the entire technology sector, particularly the personal computer industry.

Intel also said second-quarter expenses are expected to be 7 percent to 9 percent above the $1.3 billion it recorded in the prior quarter, and second-quarter interest and other income is forecast at $170 million.

For the full year, research and development spending is projected at $2.4 billion, the tax rate for the year is expected to be unchanged at 35.5 percent and capital spending is put at $4.5 billion, Intel said.
